title: Colonies, Castas and Slavery
bigQuestion: How did colonial rule sort people into ranks, and how did people resist and change those ranks?

story.title: Sixteen Panels
story.kicker: In Mexico City around 1760, a painter is paid to paint sixteen labels for sixteen kinds of people.
paragraphs: The workshop smells of linseed oil. A painter in Mexico City has sixteen canvases leaning against the wall. A wealthy customer has ordered a full set of casta paintings. Each canvas will show a family: a father, a mother and a child. Along the bottom of each, the painter will letter a label. The label names the parents' groups and gives a name to the child's group.

He starts with the first panel. A Spanish father and an Indigenous mother stand in a bright room with their small son. The label reads: from Spaniard and Indian, mestizo. On the next canvas, a Spanish father and an African mother hold a daughter. The label reads: from Spaniard and Black, mulato. Panel by panel, the labels grow longer and stranger, naming mixtures of mixtures.

The painter works carefully. He paints fine clothes on the families near the start of the set. Toward the end, the clothes grow plainer, the rooms poorer, and some families argue. The customer did not ask for real portraits of real neighbors. He asked for a picture of an idea: that people could be sorted by ancestry into ranks, with Spaniards at the top.

Outside the workshop, real life is messier. The painter's own street is full of people whose families mix every group on the canvases. Some rich merchants have mixed ancestry. Some Spaniards are poor. People often describe themselves differently to different officials. The paintings will be shipped to Spain, where collectors will look at them as a picture of New Spain. What they show is how the rulers wished society looked, not exactly how it was.
story.think: The painter was paid to paint an idea about people. Why might the people who held power want pictures like these to exist?

lessons.title: Spain and Portugal Divide the Americas
lessons.mainIdea: After 1492, Spain and Portugal claimed most of Central and South America and set up colonies ruled from Europe.
reading: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean. Two years later, in the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494, Spain and Portugal agreed on a line to divide the lands they expected to claim. Portugal received the eastern part, which became Brazil. Spain claimed most of the rest. The peoples who already lived there were not asked.

A *colony* is a land ruled by a distant country. Spain conquered the Aztec capital in 1521 and began the conquest of the Inca in 1532. It ruled its huge American lands through *viceroyalties*. Each was led by a viceroy, who governed in the king's name. The Viceroyalty of New Spain was ruled from Mexico City. The Viceroyalty of Peru was ruled from Lima.

Colonies were meant to make money for the ruling country. Silver was the great prize. In 1545, Spanish colonists began mining a huge silver mountain at Potosi, in today's Bolivia. Brazil grew rich from sugar and, later, gold. Catholic missionaries also came to spread their faith. Some protected Indigenous people from abuse, while mission life also pressed Indigenous people to give up their own beliefs.

words.d: a land ruled by a distant country
large regions of Spanish America, each ruled by a viceroy in the king's name
people sent to spread a religion to others

look.title: A Line on a Map
look.text: Picture two kings in Europe drawing a line down a map of lands they have barely seen. One side goes to Spain and the other to Portugal. Millions of people live in those lands, speaking hundreds of languages. None of them has signed the treaty.
look.prompt: What does this scene show about how colonial rulers thought about the peoples already living in the Americas?

check.q: What was a viceroyalty?
choices: A farm owned by an Indigenous family
A church school for missionaries
A large region ruled by a viceroy in the king's name
A treaty between two European kings
check.why: Spain governed its American lands through viceroyalties, each led by a viceroy.

check.q: Which land did Portugal receive after the Treaty of Tordesillas?
choices: Mexico
Peru
The Caribbean islands
The eastern part, which became Brazil
check.why: The reading says Portugal received the eastern part, which became Brazil, and Spain claimed most of the rest.

check.q: What was the main purpose of colonies for the ruling country?
choices: To make money, for example from silver and sugar
To give Indigenous peoples self-rule
To end slavery in Europe
To build roads for private travelers
check.why: Colonies were meant to make money. Potosi silver and Brazilian sugar are examples.

lessons.title: The Encomienda
lessons.mainIdea: The encomienda gave Spanish colonists the right to Indigenous people's labor and tribute, and it led to terrible abuse.
reading: After the conquest, the Spanish crown rewarded many conquerors with an *encomienda*. This was a grant of the labor and tribute of the Indigenous people in a certain area. In return, the holder, called an encomendero, was supposed to protect them and teach them Christianity. In law, the Indigenous people were not his property. In practice, many encomenderos worked people very hard and punished them cruelly.

At the same time, diseases from Europe, such as smallpox and measles, spread through the Americas. Indigenous peoples had no earlier contact with these illnesses. Terrible *epidemics* killed a very large share of the population in the 1500s. Scholars debate the exact numbers, but in many regions most people died within a few generations. War, forced labor and hunger made the losses worse.

Other forms of forced labor followed. In Peru, Spanish officials took over the old Inca mit'a. They used it to send Indigenous men in turns to work in the silver mines of Potosi, where many died. Indigenous communities pushed back. They filed lawsuits in Spanish courts, fled, and sometimes rose up. In 1780, Tupac Amaru II led a large revolt in Peru against colonial abuses.

words.d: a Spanish grant of the labor and tribute of Indigenous people in an area
outbreaks of disease that spread to many people at once
work people must do against their will

look.title: The Law and the Field
look.text: On paper, the law says: the encomendero must protect the people and may not own them. In the field, a village elder tells a priest that the men are gone for weeks at a time and the children have too little to eat. The encomendero lives far away and rarely visits.
look.prompt: Why can a law say one thing while life on the ground is very different? Who could enforce the law?

check.q: What did an encomienda give a Spanish colonist?
choices: Ownership of a silver mine in Spain
The labor and tribute of Indigenous people in an area
A seat on the king's council
Freedom from all taxes
check.why: An encomienda was a grant of Indigenous people's labor and tribute. The holder was supposed to protect them.

check.q: Why did European diseases kill so many Indigenous people?
choices: They had no doctors of their own
They lived only in cities
They had no earlier contact with those illnesses
They refused all food from Europe
check.why: The reading says Indigenous peoples had no earlier contact with diseases like smallpox, so epidemics spread widely.

check.q: How did Spanish officials use the old Inca mit'a?
choices: To build new roads for chasqui runners
To fill storehouses for hungry families
To pay Indigenous workers high wages
To send Indigenous men in turns to the silver mines of Potosi
check.why: Spanish officials took over mit'a and used it to send men in turns to the Potosi mines.

lessons.title: Voices Against Abuse
lessons.mainIdea: Some Spaniards, like Bartolome de las Casas, argued against the abuse of Indigenous people, and the crown passed laws to limit it.
reading: Bartolome de las Casas came to the Caribbean as a young colonist and held Indigenous laborers himself. Around 1514 he changed his mind. He gave up his laborers, became a Dominican friar, and spent about fifty years speaking against the cruelty he had seen. He argued that Indigenous people were fully human, with rights to their lands and freedom.

Las Casas argued with other scholars in Spain. In a famous debate at Valladolid in 1550 and 1551, he faced Juan Gines de Sepulveda. Sepulveda claimed that conquest was just. Las Casas said it was not. His voice helped push the king to pass the *New Laws* of 1542. These laws aimed to end new encomiendas and to stop the enslavement of Indigenous people.

The New Laws had limited effect. Colonists protested so strongly that parts were soon softened. Las Casas also has a mixed record. Early on, he suggested bringing enslaved Africans to spare Indigenous workers. He later wrote that he deeply regretted this. His life shows how a *reformer* can change his views and still leave a complicated legacy.

words.d: Spanish laws of 1542 meant to limit the encomienda and ban enslaving Indigenous people
a person who works to change a system to make it fairer
a member of a Catholic religious order who lives by vows and often preaches

look.title: A Friar's Warning
look.text: Las Casas described Indigenous people as gentle and patient, and he accused the Spanish of treating them with a cruelty greater than wild animals. He wrote to warn the future king about what was happening in the Indies.
look.cite: Bartolome de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, 1552 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Las Casas wanted to shock the king into action. How might that goal affect how he wrote? What makes his account still important?

check.q: What were the New Laws of 1542?
choices: Spanish laws meant to limit the encomienda and ban enslaving Indigenous people
Portuguese laws that divided Brazil
Laws that created the casta paintings
Laws that ended slavery in all colonies
check.why: The New Laws aimed to end new encomiendas and stop the enslavement of Indigenous people.

check.q: What did Las Casas argue in the debate at Valladolid?
choices: That conquest was always just
That the conquest was not just and Indigenous people had rights
That colonists should get more encomiendas
That Spain should give Brazil to Portugal
check.why: Las Casas argued against Sepulveda, who claimed conquest was just.

check.q: Why does the reading call Las Casas's legacy complicated?
choices: He never changed his views
He supported Sepulveda at Valladolid
He first suggested bringing enslaved Africans, which he later regretted
He wrote the casta paintings' labels
check.why: The reading says Las Casas early on suggested bringing enslaved Africans and later deeply regretted it.

lessons.title: Peninsulares and Criollos
lessons.mainIdea: In Spanish America, people born in Spain held top posts, and American-born Spaniards resented being ranked below them.
reading: In a Spanish colonial city, two men of Spanish families might live on the same street. One was born in Spain. He was a *peninsular*, from the Iberian Peninsula. The other was born in Mexico City. He was a *criollo*, or creole. Both claimed Spanish ancestry. But the crown often gave the highest posts, such as viceroy, bishop and top judge, to peninsulares.

Criollos were often rich. They owned land, mines and businesses, and many were well educated. Still, they felt shut out of the highest offices, especially in the late 1700s, when Spain sent more officials from Spain. Over time, many criollos began to think of themselves as Americans more than Spaniards. Their frustration later helped fuel movements for independence in the early 1800s.

This ranking is part of a larger *social hierarchy*. Birthplace, ancestry, wealth, religion and job all shaped a person's place. The crown and church kept careful records of births and marriages that often listed a person's group. Portuguese Brazil had its own ranks, with people born in Portugal at the top and enslaved Africans at the bottom.

words.d: a person in Spanish America who was born in Spain
a person of Spanish ancestry born in the Americas; also called a creole
a ranking of groups in a society by status and power

look.title: Two Cousins
look.text: Two cousins share a grandfather in Spain. One is born in Seville and sails to Mexico as a young man. The other is born in Mexico City. Both study law. When a high judge's post opens, the cousin born in Seville gets it.
look.prompt: Which cousin is the peninsular and which is the criollo? How might the criollo cousin feel, and why?

check.q: What was a criollo?
choices: A person born in Spain living in the Americas
A person of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry
An enslaved worker in a silver mine
A person of Spanish ancestry born in the Americas
check.why: Criollos were of Spanish ancestry but born in the Americas. Peninsulares were born in Spain.

check.q: Why did many criollos feel frustrated?
choices: The top posts often went to people born in Spain
They were not allowed to own land
They were forced to work in mines
They had no access to education
check.why: The reading says criollos were often rich and educated but felt shut out of the highest offices.

check.q: Which things shaped a person's place in the colonial hierarchy?
choices: Only a person's height
Birthplace, ancestry, wealth, religion and job
Only which city a person lived in
Only a person's age
check.why: The reading lists birthplace, ancestry, wealth, religion and job as shaping a person's place.

lessons.title: Mixed Societies
lessons.mainIdea: Colonial Latin America grew into mixed societies of Spanish, Indigenous and African people, and the law ranked these groups.
reading: Spanish America was never only Spanish. Indigenous people were the largest group in many regions for centuries. Africans, most brought by force, formed large communities, especially near the coasts. Over generations, many families mixed. A *mestizo* was a person of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry. A mulato was a person of Spanish and African ancestry. Many other combinations had names.

The Spanish used the word *castas* for people of mixed ancestry. Colonial law and custom ranked these groups. People of mixed ancestry often paid different taxes, could be barred from some schools, guilds and church posts, and faced limits on carrying weapons. Indigenous people lived under their own set of laws, with their own towns and leaders, and paid tribute to the crown.

The labels were not as fixed as the laws suggest. A person could be written down as one group in a baptism record and another in a marriage record. Wealth, clothing, language and friends could change how others saw someone. In the late 1700s, some people even paid the crown for official papers that raised their status. Historians see these changes as signs that the system was often bent by the people inside it.

words.d: a person of mixed Spanish and Indigenous ancestry
the colonial Spanish name for people of mixed ancestry and the ranks given to them
the people a person is descended from

look.title: One Person, Two Records
look.text: A church record from 1745 lists a baby girl as mestiza. In 1765, her marriage record lists her as espanola, or Spanish. She has not changed. But her family has become richer, and the priest who wrote the second record knew them well.
look.prompt: What does this example tell you about how fixed the casta labels really were?

check.q: What was a mestizo?
choices: A person of Spanish and African ancestry
A person born in Spain
A person of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry
A Portuguese sugar planter
check.why: The reading defines a mestizo as a person of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry. Mulato meant Spanish and African ancestry.

check.q: How could the casta system limit people of mixed ancestry?
choices: It required them to live in Spain
It forced them to become viceroys
It gave them the highest government offices
It could bar them from some schools, guilds and church posts
check.why: The reading says people of mixed ancestry could be barred from some schools, guilds and church posts.

check.q: What evidence shows casta labels could change?
choices: The same person could be listed as different groups in different records
Every person kept one label from birth to death
Labels were printed on coins
Only the king could write a label
check.why: The reading says a person could appear as one group in a baptism record and another in a marriage record.

lessons.title: The Casta Paintings
lessons.mainIdea: Casta paintings of the 1700s showed an idealized ranking of mixed families, and historians read them as ideas, not snapshots.
reading: In the 1700s, painters in New Spain made sets of *casta paintings*. A set was often sixteen panels. Each panel showed a mother, a father and a child, with a label naming each person's group. The painter Miguel Cabrera painted a famous set in 1763. Many sets were sent to Spain, where people were curious about life in the Americas.

The paintings follow a pattern. Families at the start of a set, with Spanish ancestry, often wear fine clothes in pleasant homes. Families later in the set, farther from Spanish ancestry, often look poorer. Some panels show quarrels. The paintings also show food, fruit, clothing and trades of the colony in rich detail, so they are useful for other kinds of history too.

Historians treat casta paintings as *primary sources* that show an idea, not a photograph of real life. They show how colonial elites wanted to explain and rank a mixed society. Some scholars also see pride in them, a way for criollo painters to show the richness of their homeland. Reading them well means asking who made them, who paid for them, and whom they left out.

words.d: sets of 1700s paintings from New Spain showing families labeled by mixed ancestry
documents or objects made at the time being studied
the small group with the most wealth, power or status in a society

look.title: Reading a Panel
look.text: In one panel, a Spanish father in a lace collar stands beside an Indigenous mother in a woven huipil blouse. Their son holds a basket of fruit. The room has a carved chest and a painted screen. A label at the bottom names the three groups.
look.prompt: What does this panel want a viewer in Spain to believe? What real details of colonial life can you still learn from it?

check.q: What did a typical casta painting show?
choices: A map of the Treaty of Tordesillas
A mother, father and child with labels naming their groups
A battle between Spain and the Inca
A portrait of the king of Spain
check.why: Each panel showed a family with a label naming each person's group.

check.q: How do historians read casta paintings?
choices: As exact portraits of real families
As laws passed by the viceroy
As sources that show an idea about ranking, not a photograph of real life
As tax records
check.why: The reading says historians treat casta paintings as primary sources showing an idea held by elites.

check.q: Which painter made a famous casta set in 1763?
choices: Bartolome de las Casas
Toussaint Louverture
Guaman Poma de Ayala
Miguel Cabrera
check.why: The reading names Miguel Cabrera. Las Casas was a friar and Guaman Poma an Andean writer.

lessons.title: Twelve Million People
lessons.mainIdea: From the 1500s to the 1800s, about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships bound for the Americas.
reading: The *transatlantic slave trade* carried captive Africans across the Atlantic Ocean to the Americas. It lasted from the early 1500s to the 1860s. The SlaveVoyages database, built by historians from ship records, estimates that about 12.5 million people were forced onto ships. About 10.7 million survived the voyage. Most came from West and West-Central Africa.

Traders from Portugal, Britain, France, the Netherlands, Spain, Denmark and the Americas all took part. On the African coast they bought captives, often taken in wars or raids, from African traders and rulers in exchange for cloth, guns, metal goods and other items. Some African states grew rich from the trade. Others were torn apart by it. Many Africans resisted capture and fought back.

The voyage was called the *Middle Passage*. People were chained below deck in crowded, airless spaces for weeks or months. Disease, hunger and brutality killed well over a million people at sea. Captives sometimes rose up on ships or refused to eat. Those who arrived were sold in ports across the Americas. Most were sent to work on plantations.

words.d: the forced shipping of captive Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas
the voyage across the Atlantic on which captive Africans were carried
large farms that grew one cash crop, often worked by enslaved people

look.title: Where Captives Arrived
look.cite: SlaveVoyages, Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, estimates of arrivals, 1501-1866
look.prompt: Which region received the most captives? About how many times more went to Brazil than to mainland North America?

check.q: About how many Africans were forced onto ships in the transatlantic slave trade?
choices: About 12.5 million
About 1 million
About 50 million
About 400,000
check.why: The SlaveVoyages database estimates about 12.5 million people were forced onto ships, and about 10.7 million survived.

check.q: What was the Middle Passage?
choices: A road through the Andes
The voyage across the Atlantic for captive Africans
A trade route from Spain to Asia
A canal in Tenochtitlan
check.why: The Middle Passage was the crossing on which captives were chained below deck for weeks or months.

check.q: According to the data, which region received the most captives?
choices: Mainland North America
Dutch Caribbean
Brazil
French Caribbean
check.why: The SlaveVoyages estimates show about 4.8 million arrivals in Brazil, far more than any other region.

lessons.title: Slavery in Brazil and the Caribbean
lessons.mainIdea: Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean depended on enslaved Africans, and the work was so deadly that owners kept buying more captives.
reading: On a Caribbean island in the 1700s, a *sugar mill* runs day and night at harvest time. Enslaved workers cut cane in the hot fields, then feed it into rollers and boil the juice in huge kettles. Burns and crushed limbs are common. Sugar was the main crop that drew enslaved Africans to Brazil and to islands like Jamaica, Barbados and Saint-Domingue.

The work was so harsh that many enslaved people died young. In many sugar colonies, deaths outnumbered births. Planters found it cheaper to buy new captives than to improve conditions. This is why far more Africans were shipped to Brazil and the Caribbean than to North America. In Saint-Domingue, by the late 1700s, enslaved people made up about nine out of ten people in the colony.

Enslaved people built lives and cultures under this pressure. They kept African languages, music, foods and faiths, and blended them with new ones. Religions such as Candomble in Brazil and Vodou in Haiti grew from African traditions mixed with Catholic practices. In Brazil, enslaved people could sometimes buy their freedom, so a large free Black population grew there. Freedom, though, did not mean equality.

words.d: a place where sugarcane is crushed and its juice is boiled into sugar
a crop grown to sell, not for the farmer's family to eat
a Brazilian religion that grew from West African traditions

look.title: A Survivor's Account
look.text: Olaudah Equiano, who wrote that he was taken from West Africa as a child, described the hold of the slave ship. He told of the crowding, the heat and the smell, the cries of the sick, and his wish to die rather than go on.
look.cite: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, 1789 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Equiano published his book in London while people were arguing about ending the slave trade. How might his account have affected readers?

check.q: What was a cash crop?
choices: A crop grown only for the family to eat
A crop used to pay the Inca
A crop planted in chinampas
A crop grown to sell
check.why: A cash crop is grown to sell. Sugar was the main cash crop in Brazil and the Caribbean.

check.q: Why were so many captives shipped to sugar colonies?
choices: Harsh work killed so many people that planters kept buying more
Sugar plantations needed very few workers
Enslaved people there lived longer than anywhere else
Laws there banned buying new captives
check.why: The reading says deaths outnumbered births in many sugar colonies, so planters kept buying new captives.

check.q: Which religion grew from African traditions in Brazil?
choices: The Popol Vuh
Candomble
The encomienda
Tawantinsuyu
check.why: Candomble in Brazil grew from West African traditions mixed with Catholic practices.

lessons.title: Slavery in the United States
lessons.mainIdea: Fewer captives came to North America, but slavery there grew through births to about four million people by 1860.
reading: About 400,000 captive Africans were brought to mainland North America, a small share of the whole trade. Yet by 1860 there were nearly four million enslaved people in the United States. The difference came from natural increase: births outnumbered deaths there. Slavery in the United States was *hereditary*. A child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved for life.

Enslaved people grew tobacco, rice and, above all, cotton. After Eli Whitney's cotton gin of 1793 made cleaning cotton faster, cotton spread across the Deep South. Enslaved families were often split apart by sale. Laws in many Southern states made it a crime to teach enslaved people to read. The United States banned bringing in new captives from abroad in 1808, but the trade within the country kept growing.

Enslaved people resisted in many ways. Some worked slowly, broke tools or ran away. Some, like Harriet Tubman, escaped and returned to lead others to freedom. Others kept faith, family and songs alive in secret. People who opposed slavery were called *abolitionists*. Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 and became one of the most famous abolitionist speakers and writers.

words.d: passed down from parent to child
people who worked to end slavery
population growth that happens when births outnumber deaths

look.title: Enslaved People in the United States
look.cite: U.S. Census Bureau, decennial censuses of 1790, 1820, 1840 and 1860 (rounded)
look.prompt: About how much did the enslaved population grow from 1790 to 1860? What does the chapter say caused that growth?

check.q: What does hereditary slavery mean?
choices: Slavery ended after seven years
Only prisoners of war were enslaved
A child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved for life
People could choose to become enslaved
check.why: Hereditary means passed from parent to child. In the United States, children of enslaved mothers were enslaved.

check.q: Why did the enslaved population in the United States grow so large?
choices: Most captives in the whole trade went to North America
Slavery was not hereditary there
The trade from Africa grew after 1808
Births outnumbered deaths, so it grew by natural increase
check.why: Only about 400,000 captives came, but natural increase raised the number to nearly four million by 1860.

check.q: Who escaped slavery in 1838 and became a famous abolitionist speaker?
choices: Frederick Douglass
Eli Whitney
Miguel Cabrera
Tupac Amaru II
check.why: Frederick Douglass escaped in 1838 and became a leading abolitionist speaker and writer.

lessons.title: Maroons and Everyday Resistance
lessons.mainIdea: Enslaved people resisted in every colony, from quiet daily acts to whole free communities of runaways called maroons.
reading: Deep in the hills of northeast Brazil in the 1600s stood Palmares. It was a *quilombo*, a settlement of people who had escaped slavery. Palmares grew to thousands of people and lasted for most of the century. Its people farmed, traded and defended their towns against many attacks. Portuguese forces destroyed it in 1694. Its last leader, Zumbi, was killed in 1695. Brazil honors him today with a Black Consciousness Day on November 20.

Communities of escaped people were called *maroons* in English. They formed in Jamaica, Suriname, Colombia, Florida and many other places. In Jamaica, maroon fighters forced the British to sign treaties in 1739 recognizing their towns. In Colombia, San Basilio de Palenque was founded by people who escaped slavery and still exists today.

Most resistance was quieter. Enslaved people slowed work, broke tools, pretended to be ill, or ran away for short times. They kept their names, languages and faiths. Parents taught children their family history. Historians call these everyday acts *resistance* because they pushed back against a system that tried to control every part of life.

words.d: a Brazilian settlement of people who escaped slavery
people who escaped slavery and formed free communities
actions taken to push back against control or injustice

look.title: Many Ways to Push Back
look.text: Scene 1: A woman teaches her grandchildren a song in Yoruba every night. Scene 2: A group of men slip into the mountains and build a hidden village. Scene 3: Workers in a cane field all move slowly together whenever the overseer turns away.
look.prompt: How is each scene a form of resistance? Which do you think was most dangerous, and why?

check.q: What was a quilombo?
choices: A Spanish silver mine
A Brazilian settlement of people who escaped slavery
A sugar mill in Jamaica
A church record of baptisms
check.why: A quilombo, like Palmares, was a settlement of people who had escaped slavery in Brazil.

check.q: Who was Zumbi?
choices: A Spanish viceroy
A Haitian general
The last leader of Palmares
An Inca emperor
check.why: Zumbi was the last leader of Palmares. Brazil honors him on November 20.

check.q: Which of these is an example of everyday resistance?
choices: Signing the Treaty of Tordesillas
Buying an encomienda
Painting a casta set
Keeping one's own name, language and faith
check.why: The reading lists keeping names, languages and faiths as everyday resistance.

lessons.title: The Haitian Revolution
lessons.mainIdea: From 1791 to 1804, enslaved people in Saint-Domingue overthrew slavery and French rule and founded Haiti.
reading: Saint-Domingue, the French colony on the western part of the island of Hispaniola, was the richest colony in the Caribbean. It produced huge amounts of sugar and coffee. About half a million enslaved people worked there. In August 1791 they rose up in a massive revolt in the northern plain. It became the *Haitian Revolution*, the only revolt of enslaved people in history that created a new nation.

The war was long and complex. Spain and Britain sent troops. In 1793 and 1794, French officials and then the French government in Paris ended slavery in the colony. *Toussaint Louverture*, a formerly enslaved man, became the leading general and governor. When Napoleon sent a large army in 1802 to restore French control, Toussaint was captured and shipped to France, where he died in prison in 1803.

Jean-Jacques Dessalines led the final fight. Yellow fever and fierce resistance destroyed much of the French army. On January 1, 1804, Dessalines declared the independence of Haiti, the second independent nation in the Americas after the United States. The war was brutal on all sides. Afterward, many nations refused to recognize Haiti, and in 1825 France forced it to pay a huge *indemnity* in return for recognition.

words.d: the 1791 to 1804 uprising that ended slavery and French rule in Saint-Domingue
a formerly enslaved general who led the Haitian Revolution until his capture in 1802
a payment demanded to make up for a loss

look.title: A Declaration of Rights
look.text: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 1, 1948
look.prompt: This line was written in 1948, long after 1804. How did the people of Haiti act on this idea more than a century before it was written?

check.q: What made the Haitian Revolution unique?
choices: It was the only revolt of enslaved people that created a new nation
It was the first war fought in Europe
It restored slavery in the Caribbean
It made Haiti part of Spain
check.why: The reading says it was the only revolt of enslaved people in history that created a new nation.

check.q: What happened to Toussaint Louverture?
choices: He became king of France
He was captured, shipped to France and died in prison
He founded Palmares
He signed the Treaty of Tordesillas
check.why: Napoleon's forces captured Toussaint in 1802; he died in a French prison in 1803.

check.q: When did Haiti declare independence?
choices: August 1791
January 1, 1804
check.why: Dessalines declared Haiti's independence on January 1, 1804. The revolt began in August 1791.

lessons.title: Abolition and Its Legacies
lessons.mainIdea: Slavery was abolished across the Americas between the 1790s and 1888, but its effects on inequality lasted long after.
reading: *Abolition* means ending slavery by law. It came country by country. Mexico abolished slavery in 1829. Britain ended it in most of its colonies in 1834. In the United States, the Civil War led to the Thirteenth Amendment, adopted in 1865. Illinois was the first state to ratify it, on February 1, 1865. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end slavery, with the Golden Law of May 13, 1888.

Abolition came from many forces. Enslaved people resisted and escaped. Abolitionists, Black and white, wrote, spoke and organized. Religious groups, such as Quakers, called slavery a sin. Some economists argued that free labor worked better. Wars and revolutions also broke slavery apart. Historians still debate how much each of these causes mattered in each place.

Freedom did not bring equality. Formerly enslaved people often got no land and faced unfair laws, low pay and violence. Across Latin America, the old ranking by ancestry left lasting gaps in wealth and schooling. Scholars and citizens today debate how large these *legacies* are and what, if anything, should be done. They agree that the history helps explain patterns of inequality that can still be seen.

check.q: Which was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery?
choices: Mexico, in 1829
The United States, in 1865
Haiti, in 1804
Brazil, in 1888
check.why: Brazil's Golden Law of May 13, 1888 made it the last country in the Americas to end slavery.

check.q: Which state was the first to ratify the Thirteenth Amendment?
choices: Illinois
Virginia
New York
Georgia
check.why: The reading says Illinois ratified the Thirteenth Amendment first, on February 1, 1865.

check.q: What is a legacy of slavery, as the reading uses the word?
choices: A law that ends slavery
An effect of the past, such as gaps in wealth, that continues later
A ship that carried captives
A painting of a family
check.why: Legacies are effects of the past that continue. The reading names lasting gaps in wealth and schooling.

review.q: What was the difference between a peninsular and a criollo?
choices: A peninsular was Indigenous; a criollo was African
A peninsular was a priest; a criollo was a soldier
A peninsular was born in Spain; a criollo was of Spanish ancestry born in the Americas
They meant the same thing
review.why: Both had Spanish ancestry, but peninsulares were born in Spain and often got the top posts.

review.q: How was the encomienda different from the New Laws?
choices: The encomienda ended slavery; the New Laws started it
Both were Portuguese laws for Brazil
Both created the casta paintings
The encomienda granted Indigenous labor; the New Laws tried to limit it
review.why: The encomienda granted labor and tribute, and the New Laws of 1542 aimed to end new grants.

review.q: What is the best way to use a casta painting as evidence?
choices: As a source that shows how elites wanted to rank society
As an exact photograph of a real family
As proof that labels never changed
As a record of the slave trade
review.why: Historians read casta paintings as primary sources showing an idea, not as snapshots of real life.

review.q: Which region received the most enslaved Africans?
choices: Mainland North America
Brazil
Mexico
Peru
review.why: SlaveVoyages estimates about 4.8 million arrivals in Brazil, the most of any region.

review.q: Why did slavery in the United States grow even though few captives arrived there?
choices: Most of the whole trade went there
The United States kept importing captives until 1888
Slavery was hereditary and births outnumbered deaths
Enslaved people there could not have children
review.why: About 400,000 captives arrived, but hereditary slavery and natural increase led to nearly four million by 1860.

review.q: Palmares and the Jamaican maroon towns were both examples of what?
choices: Spanish viceroyalties
Sugar mills owned by planters
Schools for noble children
Free communities formed by people who escaped slavery
review.why: Both were maroon communities, called quilombos in Brazil, formed by people who escaped slavery.

choices: The Haitian Revolution begins
Brazil abolishes slavery
The Thirteenth Amendment is adopted
Cuba abolishes slavery
review.why: The Haitian Revolution began in 1791, long before 1865, 1886 and 1888.

review.q: According to the chapter, what do historians still debate about abolition?
choices: Whether slavery ever existed
How much each cause, like resistance or activism, mattered in each place
Whether Brazil ended slavery at all
Whether Haiti became independent
